case_info.scenario: A man in his 30s presented with a painful ulcer on the ventral aspect of the penile shaft that had appeared 3 months before. His medical history included recent unprotected sexual intercourse 2 months prior to consultation and recurrent self-healing ulcers on both the ventral and dorsal sides of the penis over the past 3 months. Physical examination disclosed discrete penile swelling with an indurated yellowish plaque diffusely involving the ventral surface. A well-circumscribed, round-shaped, 10 × 8-mm diameter, nonexudative ulcer on the more proximal area of the plaque was also noted (Figure 1A). In addition, 3 round-shaped scars, corresponding to previously resolved ulcerations, were observed on the penile dorsum. No regional lymphadenopathy or other mucocutaneous lesions were detected. Results of a complete standard laboratory workup was normal. Results of polymerase chain reaction for herpesvirus types 1 and 2,Treponema pallidum, andChlamydia, along with bacterial cultures of the ulcer, were all negative. Results of serology for syphilis, HIV, and hepatitis C and hepatitis B virus were also negative. A cutaneous biopsy obtained from the ulcer’s periphery was performed for histopathological examination and cultures (Figure 1B).

case_info.caption: A, A well-circumscribed, round-shaped, 10 × 8-mm diameter, nonexudative ulcer surrounded by a discrete penile swelling and an indurated yellowish plaque in the ventral aspect of the penile shaft. case_info.explanation: A. Sclerosing lipogranuloma of the penis Histopathological analysis revealed a diffuse dermal hyaline fibrosis with cystic spaces of variable size, some of them surrounded by histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells adopting a characteristic Swiss-cheese pattern that extended to the subcutaneous tissue (Figure 1B andFigure 2). Scattered patchy neutrophilic infiltrates with focal areas of dermal necrosis and occasional plasma cells were observed. In other areas, discrete focal foreign-body granulomatous reaction with histiocytes containing intracytoplasmic lipid vacuoles, lymphocytes, and plasma cells were noted (Figure 2). Findings of periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott, and modified Ziehl–Neelsen staining, along with bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures, were all negative. On detailed anamnesis, the patient reported that 2 years before he had received several injections of kanamycin ointment, containing paraffin, for penis augmentation. He refused further treatment and was lost to follow-up. Sclerosing lipogranuloma of the penis (SLP) is a foreign-body granulomatous reaction to lipidic substances injected into the dermis and subcutaneous tissue to enlarge genitalia.1-4The most commonly injected materials include paraffin and silicone (resulting in conditions known as paraffinoma and siliconoma, respectively), followed by olive oil, motor oil, cod liver oil, or vaseline.1-4There is an increased incidence in patients from Thailand, Korea, and Eastern Europe, where these procedures remain prevalent, especially among incarcerated individuals.1Cases of SLP due to self-injection of kanamycin ointment are almost exclusively reported in Romania,5the origin country of this patient. Penile injections are typically administered in a nonstandardized manner by nonprofessional individuals or by patients themselves.1 SLP usually affects sexually active men in their third decade of life.1Symptoms tend to appear 1 to 2 years after the injection, with genital erythema, edema, and swelling. They progress to persistent, painless preputial masses or nodules. Injected material may migrate locoregionally, causing suprapubic and scrotal involvement, acquired phimosis, or lymphangitis. Chronic inflammation finally leads to the development of foreign-body granulomas, presenting as indurated, occasionally ulcerated, yellowish fibrotic penile plaques, also known aswoody penis, as seen in this case. These patients often experience painful erections, severely impacting their quality of life.1-4 Diagnosis is usually established on the basis of a detailed anamnesis and characteristic clinicopathological features. Significant diagnostic delays occur because patients frequently postpone seeking medical attention and typically deny such practices when questioned.1-4Histologically, SLP shows marked sclerosis in the reticular dermis and subcutis with numerous vacuoles of various sizes surrounded by lymphohistiocytic infiltrates and foreign-body multinucleated giant cells, creating a characteristic Swiss-cheese pattern.1-4 SLP must be differentiated from autoimmune syndrome induced by adjuvants, triggered by the injection of foreign substances, such as silicone or aluminum, leading to immune-mediated conditions that can manifest as morphealike plaques at the injection sites. Histologically, lesions are characterized by deep dermal sclerosis lacking vacuoles surrounded by multinucleated giant cells.6,7Atypical mycobacterial cutaneous infections, often resulting from contaminated injection materials, typically present with dermal suppurative granulomas, which differ from the foreign-body granulomatous reaction seen in SLP.8Additionally, necrobiosis lipoidica involving the genitalia, though rare, exhibits a characteristic interstitial and palisading necrobiotic granulomatous tissue reaction, sharply contrasting with the Swiss-cheese pattern of SLP.9Along with the histopathological features, the absence of systemic symptoms and isolation of infectious microorganisms permitted to exclude these diagnoses. Treatment of SLP is challenging. Surgical removal of the inoculated material is the treatment of choice; nonetheless, it is often unfeasible or results in unacceptable sequelae. Moreover, these operations are complex, time-consuming plastic and reconstructive procedures, sometimes requiring multiple stages. Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging of the penis and scrotum is crucial for surgical planning to ensure complete removal of injected materials and granulomatous tissue. Alternatively, isolated cases treated with intralesional corticosteroids have shown acceptable outcomes. Systemic corticosteroids may provide temporary relief but have a high recurrence rate when used alone. In cases of necrosis, urgent debridement is required to prevent further complications.1,3

dialogue_history.text: Sclerosing lipogranuloma is a consideration, but the chronicity, recurrent ulcers, and indurated yellowish plaque are highly characteristic of donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) in this sexual history context. Donovanosis often shows dermal fibrosis and cystic spaces histologically, and the negative routine PCR/cultures do not rule it out since it requires specific staining for Donovan bodies. A deeper histologic review for intracellular organisms (Wright-Giemsa stain) or molecular testing for Klebsiella granulomatis should be prioritized before committing to a noninfectious diagnosis.

  score low.)

  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A. Sclerosing lipogranuloma of the penis Histopathological analysis revealed a diffuse dermal hyaline fibrosis with cystic spaces of variable size, some of them surrounded by histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells adopting a characteristic Swiss-cheese pattern that extended to the subcutaneous tissue (Figure 1B andFigure 2). Scattered patchy neutrophilic infiltrates with focal areas of dermal necrosis and occasional plasma cells were observed. In other areas, discrete focal foreign-body granulomatous reaction with histiocytes containing intracytoplasmic lipid vacuoles, lymphocytes, and plasma cells were noted (Figure 2). Findings of periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott, and modified Ziehl–Neelsen staining, along with bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures, were all negative. On detailed anamnesis, the patient reported that 2 years before he had received several injections of kanamycin ointment, containing paraffin, for penis augmentation. He refused further treatment and was lost to follow-up. Sclerosing lipogranuloma of the penis (SLP) is a foreign-body granulomatous reaction to lipidic substances injected into the dermis and subcutaneous tissue to enlarge genitalia.1-4The most commonly injected materials include paraffin and silicone (resulting in conditions known as paraffinoma and siliconoma, respectively), followed by olive oil, motor oil, cod liver oil, or vaseline.1-4There is an increased incidence in patients from Thailand, Korea, and Eastern Europe, where these procedures remain prevalent, especially among incarcerated individuals.1Cases of SLP due to self-injection of kanamycin ointment are almost exclusively reported in Romania,5the origin country of this patient. Penile injections are typically administered in a nonstandardized manner by nonprofessional individuals or by patients themselves.1 SLP usually affects sexually active men in their third decade of life.1Symptoms tend to appear 1 to 2 years after the injection, with genital erythema, edema, and swelling. They progress to persistent, painless preputial masses or nodules. Injected material may migrate locoregionally, causing suprapubic and scrotal involvement, acquired phimosis, or lymphangitis. Chronic inflammation finally leads to the development of foreign-body granulomas, presenting as indurated, occasionally ulcerated, yellowish fibrotic penile plaques, also known aswoody penis, as seen in this case. These patients often experience painful erections, severely impacting their quality of life.1-4 Diagnosis is usually established on the basis of a detailed anamnesis and characteristic clinicopathological features. Significant diagnostic delays occur because patients frequently postpone seeking medical attention and typically deny such practices when questioned.1-4Histologically, SLP shows marked sclerosis in the reticular dermis and subcutis with numerous vacuoles of various sizes surrounded by lymphohistiocytic infiltrates and foreign-body multinucleated giant cells, creating a characteristic Swiss-cheese pattern.1-4 SLP must be differentiated from autoimmune syndrome induced by adjuvants, triggered by the injection of foreign substances, such as silicone or aluminum, leading to immune-mediated conditions that can manifest as morphealike plaques at the injection sites. Histologically, lesions are characterized by deep dermal sclerosis lacking vacuoles surrounded by multinucleated giant cells.6,7Atypical mycobacterial cutaneous infections, often resulting from contaminated injection materials, typically present with dermal suppurative granulomas, which differ from the foreign-body granulomatous reaction seen in SLP.8Additionally, necrobiosis lipoidica involving the genitalia, though rare, exhibits a characteristic interstitial and palisading necrobiotic granulomatous tissue reaction, sharply contrasting with the Swiss-cheese pattern of SLP.9Along with the histopathological features, the absence of systemic symptoms and isolation of infectious microorganisms permitted to exclude these diagnoses. Treatment of SLP is challenging. Surgical removal of the inoculated material is the treatment of choice; nonetheless, it is often unfeasible or results in unacceptable sequelae. Moreover, these operations are complex, time-consuming plastic and reconstructive procedures, sometimes requiring multiple stages. Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging of the penis and scrotum is crucial for surgical planning to ensure complete removal of injected materials and granulomatous tissue. Alternatively, isolated cases treated with intralesional corticosteroids have shown acceptable outcomes. Systemic corticosteroids may provide temporary relief but have a high recurrence rate when used alone. In cases of necrosis, urgent debridement is required to prevent further complications.1,3

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the

   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an

case_info.explanation: A. Sclerosing lipogranuloma of the penis Histopathological analysis revealed a diffuse dermal hyaline fibrosis with cystic spaces of variable size, some of them surrounded by histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells adopting a characteristic Swiss-cheese pattern that extended to the subcutaneous tissue (Figure 1B andFigure 2). Scattered patchy neutrophilic infiltrates with focal areas of dermal necrosis and occasional plasma cells were observed. In other areas, discrete focal foreign-body granulomatous reaction with histiocytes containing intracytoplasmic lipid vacuoles, lymphocytes, and plasma cells were noted (Figure 2). Findings of periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott, and modified Ziehl–Neelsen staining, along with bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures, were all negative. On detailed anamnesis, the patient reported that 2 years before he had received several injections of kanamycin ointment, containing paraffin, for penis augmentation. He refused further treatment and was lost to follow-up. Sclerosing lipogranuloma of the penis (SLP) is a foreign-body granulomatous reaction to lipidic substances injected into the dermis and subcutaneous tissue to enlarge genitalia.1-4The most commonly injected materials include paraffin and silicone (resulting in conditions known as paraffinoma and siliconoma, respectively), followed by olive oil, motor oil, cod liver oil, or vaseline.1-4There is an increased incidence in patients from Thailand, Korea, and Eastern Europe, where these procedures remain prevalent, especially among incarcerated individuals.1Cases of SLP due to self-injection of kanamycin ointment are almost exclusively reported in Romania,5the origin country of this patient. Penile injections are typically administered in a nonstandardized manner by nonprofessional individuals or by patients themselves.1 SLP usually affects sexually active men in their third decade of life.1Symptoms tend to appear 1 to 2 years after the injection, with genital erythema, edema, and swelling. They progress to persistent, painless preputial masses or nodules. Injected material may migrate locoregionally, causing suprapubic and scrotal involvement, acquired phimosis, or lymphangitis. Chronic inflammation finally leads to the development of foreign-body granulomas, presenting as indurated, occasionally ulcerated, yellowish fibrotic penile plaques, also known aswoody penis, as seen in this case. These patients often experience painful erections, severely impacting their quality of life.1-4 Diagnosis is usually established on the basis of a detailed anamnesis and characteristic clinicopathological features. Significant diagnostic delays occur because patients frequently postpone seeking medical attention and typically deny such practices when questioned.1-4Histologically, SLP shows marked sclerosis in the reticular dermis and subcutis with numerous vacuoles of various sizes surrounded by lymphohistiocytic infiltrates and foreign-body multinucleated giant cells, creating a characteristic Swiss-cheese pattern.1-4 SLP must be differentiated from autoimmune syndrome induced by adjuvants, triggered by the injection of foreign substances, such as silicone or aluminum, leading to immune-mediated conditions that can manifest as morphealike plaques at the injection sites. Histologically, lesions are characterized by deep dermal sclerosis lacking vacuoles surrounded by multinucleated giant cells.6,7Atypical mycobacterial cutaneous infections, often resulting from contaminated injection materials, typically present with dermal suppurative granulomas, which differ from the foreign-body granulomatous reaction seen in SLP.8Additionally, necrobiosis lipoidica involving the genitalia, though rare, exhibits a characteristic interstitial and palisading necrobiotic granulomatous tissue reaction, sharply contrasting with the Swiss-cheese pattern of SLP.9Along with the histopathological features, the absence of systemic symptoms and isolation of infectious microorganisms permitted to exclude these diagnoses. Treatment of SLP is challenging. Surgical removal of the inoculated material is the treatment of choice; nonetheless, it is often unfeasible or results in unacceptable sequelae. Moreover, these operations are complex, time-consuming plastic and reconstructive procedures, sometimes requiring multiple stages. Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging of the penis and scrotum is crucial for surgical planning to ensure complete removal of injected materials and granulomatous tissue. Alternatively, isolated cases treated with intralesional corticosteroids have shown acceptable outcomes. Systemic corticosteroids may provide temporary relief but have a high recurrence rate when used alone. In cases of necrosis, urgent debridement is required to prevent further complications.1,3

case_info.explanation: A. Sclerosing lipogranuloma of the penis Histopathological analysis revealed a diffuse dermal hyaline fibrosis with cystic spaces of variable size, some of them surrounded by histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells adopting a characteristic Swiss-cheese pattern that extended to the subcutaneous tissue (Figure 1B andFigure 2). Scattered patchy neutrophilic infiltrates with focal areas of dermal necrosis and occasional plasma cells were observed. In other areas, discrete focal foreign-body granulomatous reaction with histiocytes containing intracytoplasmic lipid vacuoles, lymphocytes, and plasma cells were noted (Figure 2). Findings of periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott, and modified Ziehl–Neelsen staining, along with bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures, were all negative. On detailed anamnesis, the patient reported that 2 years before he had received several injections of kanamycin ointment, containing paraffin, for penis augmentation. He refused further treatment and was lost to follow-up. Sclerosing lipogranuloma of the penis (SLP) is a foreign-body granulomatous reaction to lipidic substances injected into the dermis and subcutaneous tissue to enlarge genitalia.1-4The most commonly injected materials include paraffin and silicone (resulting in conditions known as paraffinoma and siliconoma, respectively), followed by olive oil, motor oil, cod liver oil, or vaseline.1-4There is an increased incidence in patients from Thailand, Korea, and Eastern Europe, where these procedures remain prevalent, especially among incarcerated individuals.1Cases of SLP due to self-injection of kanamycin ointment are almost exclusively reported in Romania,5the origin country of this patient. Penile injections are typically administered in a nonstandardized manner by nonprofessional individuals or by patients themselves.1 SLP usually affects sexually active men in their third decade of life.1Symptoms tend to appear 1 to 2 years after the injection, with genital erythema, edema, and swelling. They progress to persistent, painless preputial masses or nodules. Injected material may migrate locoregionally, causing suprapubic and scrotal involvement, acquired phimosis, or lymphangitis. Chronic inflammation finally leads to the development of foreign-body granulomas, presenting as indurated, occasionally ulcerated, yellowish fibrotic penile plaques, also known aswoody penis, as seen in this case. These patients often experience painful erections, severely impacting their quality of life.1-4 Diagnosis is usually established on the basis of a detailed anamnesis and characteristic clinicopathological features. Significant diagnostic delays occur because patients frequently postpone seeking medical attention and typically deny such practices when questioned.1-4Histologically, SLP shows marked sclerosis in the reticular dermis and subcutis with numerous vacuoles of various sizes surrounded by lymphohistiocytic infiltrates and foreign-body multinucleated giant cells, creating a characteristic Swiss-cheese pattern.1-4 SLP must be differentiated from autoimmune syndrome induced by adjuvants, triggered by the injection of foreign substances, such as silicone or aluminum, leading to immune-mediated conditions that can manifest as morphealike plaques at the injection sites. Histologically, lesions are characterized by deep dermal sclerosis lacking vacuoles surrounded by multinucleated giant cells.6,7Atypical mycobacterial cutaneous infections, often resulting from contaminated injection materials, typically present with dermal suppurative granulomas, which differ from the foreign-body granulomatous reaction seen in SLP.8Additionally, necrobiosis lipoidica involving the genitalia, though rare, exhibits a characteristic interstitial and palisading necrobiotic granulomatous tissue reaction, sharply contrasting with the Swiss-cheese pattern of SLP.9Along with the histopathological features, the absence of systemic symptoms and isolation of infectious microorganisms permitted to exclude these diagnoses. Treatment of SLP is challenging. Surgical removal of the inoculated material is the treatment of choice; nonetheless, it is often unfeasible or results in unacceptable sequelae. Moreover, these operations are complex, time-consuming plastic and reconstructive procedures, sometimes requiring multiple stages. Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging of the penis and scrotum is crucial for surgical planning to ensure complete removal of injected materials and granulomatous tissue. Alternatively, isolated cases treated with intralesional corticosteroids have shown acceptable outcomes. Systemic corticosteroids may provide temporary relief but have a high recurrence rate when used alone. In cases of necrosis, urgent debridement is required to prevent further complications.1,3

   Definition:

       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

case_info.explanation: A. Sclerosing lipogranuloma of the penis Histopathological analysis revealed a diffuse dermal hyaline fibrosis with cystic spaces of variable size, some of them surrounded by histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells adopting a characteristic Swiss-cheese pattern that extended to the subcutaneous tissue (Figure 1B andFigure 2). Scattered patchy neutrophilic infiltrates with focal areas of dermal necrosis and occasional plasma cells were observed. In other areas, discrete focal foreign-body granulomatous reaction with histiocytes containing intracytoplasmic lipid vacuoles, lymphocytes, and plasma cells were noted (Figure 2). Findings of periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott, and modified Ziehl–Neelsen staining, along with bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures, were all negative. On detailed anamnesis, the patient reported that 2 years before he had received several injections of kanamycin ointment, containing paraffin, for penis augmentation. He refused further treatment and was lost to follow-up. Sclerosing lipogranuloma of the penis (SLP) is a foreign-body granulomatous reaction to lipidic substances injected into the dermis and subcutaneous tissue to enlarge genitalia.1-4The most commonly injected materials include paraffin and silicone (resulting in conditions known as paraffinoma and siliconoma, respectively), followed by olive oil, motor oil, cod liver oil, or vaseline.1-4There is an increased incidence in patients from Thailand, Korea, and Eastern Europe, where these procedures remain prevalent, especially among incarcerated individuals.1Cases of SLP due to self-injection of kanamycin ointment are almost exclusively reported in Romania,5the origin country of this patient. Penile injections are typically administered in a nonstandardized manner by nonprofessional individuals or by patients themselves.1 SLP usually affects sexually active men in their third decade of life.1Symptoms tend to appear 1 to 2 years after the injection, with genital erythema, edema, and swelling. They progress to persistent, painless preputial masses or nodules. Injected material may migrate locoregionally, causing suprapubic and scrotal involvement, acquired phimosis, or lymphangitis. Chronic inflammation finally leads to the development of foreign-body granulomas, presenting as indurated, occasionally ulcerated, yellowish fibrotic penile plaques, also known aswoody penis, as seen in this case. These patients often experience painful erections, severely impacting their quality of life.1-4 Diagnosis is usually established on the basis of a detailed anamnesis and characteristic clinicopathological features. Significant diagnostic delays occur because patients frequently postpone seeking medical attention and typically deny such practices when questioned.1-4Histologically, SLP shows marked sclerosis in the reticular dermis and subcutis with numerous vacuoles of various sizes surrounded by lymphohistiocytic infiltrates and foreign-body multinucleated giant cells, creating a characteristic Swiss-cheese pattern.1-4 SLP must be differentiated from autoimmune syndrome induced by adjuvants, triggered by the injection of foreign substances, such as silicone or aluminum, leading to immune-mediated conditions that can manifest as morphealike plaques at the injection sites. Histologically, lesions are characterized by deep dermal sclerosis lacking vacuoles surrounded by multinucleated giant cells.6,7Atypical mycobacterial cutaneous infections, often resulting from contaminated injection materials, typically present with dermal suppurative granulomas, which differ from the foreign-body granulomatous reaction seen in SLP.8Additionally, necrobiosis lipoidica involving the genitalia, though rare, exhibits a characteristic interstitial and palisading necrobiotic granulomatous tissue reaction, sharply contrasting with the Swiss-cheese pattern of SLP.9Along with the histopathological features, the absence of systemic symptoms and isolation of infectious microorganisms permitted to exclude these diagnoses. Treatment of SLP is challenging. Surgical removal of the inoculated material is the treatment of choice; nonetheless, it is often unfeasible or results in unacceptable sequelae. Moreover, these operations are complex, time-consuming plastic and reconstructive procedures, sometimes requiring multiple stages. Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging of the penis and scrotum is crucial for surgical planning to ensure complete removal of injected materials and granulomatous tissue. Alternatively, isolated cases treated with intralesional corticosteroids have shown acceptable outcomes. Systemic corticosteroids may provide temporary relief but have a high recurrence rate when used alone. In cases of necrosis, urgent debridement is required to prevent further complications.1,3

case_info.explanation: A. Sclerosing lipogranuloma of the penis Histopathological analysis revealed a diffuse dermal hyaline fibrosis with cystic spaces of variable size, some of them surrounded by histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells adopting a characteristic Swiss-cheese pattern that extended to the subcutaneous tissue (Figure 1B andFigure 2). Scattered patchy neutrophilic infiltrates with focal areas of dermal necrosis and occasional plasma cells were observed. In other areas, discrete focal foreign-body granulomatous reaction with histiocytes containing intracytoplasmic lipid vacuoles, lymphocytes, and plasma cells were noted (Figure 2). Findings of periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott, and modified Ziehl–Neelsen staining, along with bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures, were all negative. On detailed anamnesis, the patient reported that 2 years before he had received several injections of kanamycin ointment, containing paraffin, for penis augmentation. He refused further treatment and was lost to follow-up. Sclerosing lipogranuloma of the penis (SLP) is a foreign-body granulomatous reaction to lipidic substances injected into the dermis and subcutaneous tissue to enlarge genitalia.1-4The most commonly injected materials include paraffin and silicone (resulting in conditions known as paraffinoma and siliconoma, respectively), followed by olive oil, motor oil, cod liver oil, or vaseline.1-4There is an increased incidence in patients from Thailand, Korea, and Eastern Europe, where these procedures remain prevalent, especially among incarcerated individuals.1Cases of SLP due to self-injection of kanamycin ointment are almost exclusively reported in Romania,5the origin country of this patient. Penile injections are typically administered in a nonstandardized manner by nonprofessional individuals or by patients themselves.1 SLP usually affects sexually active men in their third decade of life.1Symptoms tend to appear 1 to 2 years after the injection, with genital erythema, edema, and swelling. They progress to persistent, painless preputial masses or nodules. Injected material may migrate locoregionally, causing suprapubic and scrotal involvement, acquired phimosis, or lymphangitis. Chronic inflammation finally leads to the development of foreign-body granulomas, presenting as indurated, occasionally ulcerated, yellowish fibrotic penile plaques, also known aswoody penis, as seen in this case. These patients often experience painful erections, severely impacting their quality of life.1-4 Diagnosis is usually established on the basis of a detailed anamnesis and characteristic clinicopathological features. Significant diagnostic delays occur because patients frequently postpone seeking medical attention and typically deny such practices when questioned.1-4Histologically, SLP shows marked sclerosis in the reticular dermis and subcutis with numerous vacuoles of various sizes surrounded by lymphohistiocytic infiltrates and foreign-body multinucleated giant cells, creating a characteristic Swiss-cheese pattern.1-4 SLP must be differentiated from autoimmune syndrome induced by adjuvants, triggered by the injection of foreign substances, such as silicone or aluminum, leading to immune-mediated conditions that can manifest as morphealike plaques at the injection sites. Histologically, lesions are characterized by deep dermal sclerosis lacking vacuoles surrounded by multinucleated giant cells.6,7Atypical mycobacterial cutaneous infections, often resulting from contaminated injection materials, typically present with dermal suppurative granulomas, which differ from the foreign-body granulomatous reaction seen in SLP.8Additionally, necrobiosis lipoidica involving the genitalia, though rare, exhibits a characteristic interstitial and palisading necrobiotic granulomatous tissue reaction, sharply contrasting with the Swiss-cheese pattern of SLP.9Along with the histopathological features, the absence of systemic symptoms and isolation of infectious microorganisms permitted to exclude these diagnoses. Treatment of SLP is challenging. Surgical removal of the inoculated material is the treatment of choice; nonetheless, it is often unfeasible or results in unacceptable sequelae. Moreover, these operations are complex, time-consuming plastic and reconstructive procedures, sometimes requiring multiple stages. Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging of the penis and scrotum is crucial for surgical planning to ensure complete removal of injected materials and granulomatous tissue. Alternatively, isolated cases treated with intralesional corticosteroids have shown acceptable outcomes. Systemic corticosteroids may provide temporary relief but have a high recurrence rate when used alone. In cases of necrosis, urgent debridement is required to prevent further complications.1,3

case_info.explanation: A. Sclerosing lipogranuloma of the penis Histopathological analysis revealed a diffuse dermal hyaline fibrosis with cystic spaces of variable size, some of them surrounded by histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells adopting a characteristic Swiss-cheese pattern that extended to the subcutaneous tissue (Figure 1B andFigure 2). Scattered patchy neutrophilic infiltrates with focal areas of dermal necrosis and occasional plasma cells were observed. In other areas, discrete focal foreign-body granulomatous reaction with histiocytes containing intracytoplasmic lipid vacuoles, lymphocytes, and plasma cells were noted (Figure 2). Findings of periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott, and modified Ziehl–Neelsen staining, along with bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures, were all negative. On detailed anamnesis, the patient reported that 2 years before he had received several injections of kanamycin ointment, containing paraffin, for penis augmentation. He refused further treatment and was lost to follow-up. Sclerosing lipogranuloma of the penis (SLP) is a foreign-body granulomatous reaction to lipidic substances injected into the dermis and subcutaneous tissue to enlarge genitalia.1-4The most commonly injected materials include paraffin and silicone (resulting in conditions known as paraffinoma and siliconoma, respectively), followed by olive oil, motor oil, cod liver oil, or vaseline.1-4There is an increased incidence in patients from Thailand, Korea, and Eastern Europe, where these procedures remain prevalent, especially among incarcerated individuals.1Cases of SLP due to self-injection of kanamycin ointment are almost exclusively reported in Romania,5the origin country of this patient. Penile injections are typically administered in a nonstandardized manner by nonprofessional individuals or by patients themselves.1 SLP usually affects sexually active men in their third decade of life.1Symptoms tend to appear 1 to 2 years after the injection, with genital erythema, edema, and swelling. They progress to persistent, painless preputial masses or nodules. Injected material may migrate locoregionally, causing suprapubic and scrotal involvement, acquired phimosis, or lymphangitis. Chronic inflammation finally leads to the development of foreign-body granulomas, presenting as indurated, occasionally ulcerated, yellowish fibrotic penile plaques, also known aswoody penis, as seen in this case. These patients often experience painful erections, severely impacting their quality of life.1-4 Diagnosis is usually established on the basis of a detailed anamnesis and characteristic clinicopathological features. Significant diagnostic delays occur because patients frequently postpone seeking medical attention and typically deny such practices when questioned.1-4Histologically, SLP shows marked sclerosis in the reticular dermis and subcutis with numerous vacuoles of various sizes surrounded by lymphohistiocytic infiltrates and foreign-body multinucleated giant cells, creating a characteristic Swiss-cheese pattern.1-4 SLP must be differentiated from autoimmune syndrome induced by adjuvants, triggered by the injection of foreign substances, such as silicone or aluminum, leading to immune-mediated conditions that can manifest as morphealike plaques at the injection sites. Histologically, lesions are characterized by deep dermal sclerosis lacking vacuoles surrounded by multinucleated giant cells.6,7Atypical mycobacterial cutaneous infections, often resulting from contaminated injection materials, typically present with dermal suppurative granulomas, which differ from the foreign-body granulomatous reaction seen in SLP.8Additionally, necrobiosis lipoidica involving the genitalia, though rare, exhibits a characteristic interstitial and palisading necrobiotic granulomatous tissue reaction, sharply contrasting with the Swiss-cheese pattern of SLP.9Along with the histopathological features, the absence of systemic symptoms and isolation of infectious microorganisms permitted to exclude these diagnoses. Treatment of SLP is challenging. Surgical removal of the inoculated material is the treatment of choice; nonetheless, it is often unfeasible or results in unacceptable sequelae. Moreover, these operations are complex, time-consuming plastic and reconstructive procedures, sometimes requiring multiple stages. Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging of the penis and scrotum is crucial for surgical planning to ensure complete removal of injected materials and granulomatous tissue. Alternatively, isolated cases treated with intralesional corticosteroids have shown acceptable outcomes. Systemic corticosteroids may provide temporary relief but have a high recurrence rate when used alone. In cases of necrosis, urgent debridement is required to prevent further complications.1,3

* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging

   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

   Definition:

case_info.explanation: A. Sclerosing lipogranuloma of the penis Histopathological analysis revealed a diffuse dermal hyaline fibrosis with cystic spaces of variable size, some of them surrounded by histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells adopting a characteristic Swiss-cheese pattern that extended to the subcutaneous tissue (Figure 1B andFigure 2). Scattered patchy neutrophilic infiltrates with focal areas of dermal necrosis and occasional plasma cells were observed. In other areas, discrete focal foreign-body granulomatous reaction with histiocytes containing intracytoplasmic lipid vacuoles, lymphocytes, and plasma cells were noted (Figure 2). Findings of periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott, and modified Ziehl–Neelsen staining, along with bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures, were all negative. On detailed anamnesis, the patient reported that 2 years before he had received several injections of kanamycin ointment, containing paraffin, for penis augmentation. He refused further treatment and was lost to follow-up. Sclerosing lipogranuloma of the penis (SLP) is a foreign-body granulomatous reaction to lipidic substances injected into the dermis and subcutaneous tissue to enlarge genitalia.1-4The most commonly injected materials include paraffin and silicone (resulting in conditions known as paraffinoma and siliconoma, respectively), followed by olive oil, motor oil, cod liver oil, or vaseline.1-4There is an increased incidence in patients from Thailand, Korea, and Eastern Europe, where these procedures remain prevalent, especially among incarcerated individuals.1Cases of SLP due to self-injection of kanamycin ointment are almost exclusively reported in Romania,5the origin country of this patient. Penile injections are typically administered in a nonstandardized manner by nonprofessional individuals or by patients themselves.1 SLP usually affects sexually active men in their third decade of life.1Symptoms tend to appear 1 to 2 years after the injection, with genital erythema, edema, and swelling. They progress to persistent, painless preputial masses or nodules. Injected material may migrate locoregionally, causing suprapubic and scrotal involvement, acquired phimosis, or lymphangitis. Chronic inflammation finally leads to the development of foreign-body granulomas, presenting as indurated, occasionally ulcerated, yellowish fibrotic penile plaques, also known aswoody penis, as seen in this case. These patients often experience painful erections, severely impacting their quality of life.1-4 Diagnosis is usually established on the basis of a detailed anamnesis and characteristic clinicopathological features. Significant diagnostic delays occur because patients frequently postpone seeking medical attention and typically deny such practices when questioned.1-4Histologically, SLP shows marked sclerosis in the reticular dermis and subcutis with numerous vacuoles of various sizes surrounded by lymphohistiocytic infiltrates and foreign-body multinucleated giant cells, creating a characteristic Swiss-cheese pattern.1-4 SLP must be differentiated from autoimmune syndrome induced by adjuvants, triggered by the injection of foreign substances, such as silicone or aluminum, leading to immune-mediated conditions that can manifest as morphealike plaques at the injection sites. Histologically, lesions are characterized by deep dermal sclerosis lacking vacuoles surrounded by multinucleated giant cells.6,7Atypical mycobacterial cutaneous infections, often resulting from contaminated injection materials, typically present with dermal suppurative granulomas, which differ from the foreign-body granulomatous reaction seen in SLP.8Additionally, necrobiosis lipoidica involving the genitalia, though rare, exhibits a characteristic interstitial and palisading necrobiotic granulomatous tissue reaction, sharply contrasting with the Swiss-cheese pattern of SLP.9Along with the histopathological features, the absence of systemic symptoms and isolation of infectious microorganisms permitted to exclude these diagnoses. Treatment of SLP is challenging. Surgical removal of the inoculated material is the treatment of choice; nonetheless, it is often unfeasible or results in unacceptable sequelae. Moreover, these operations are complex, time-consuming plastic and reconstructive procedures, sometimes requiring multiple stages. Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging of the penis and scrotum is crucial for surgical planning to ensure complete removal of injected materials and granulomatous tissue. Alternatively, isolated cases treated with intralesional corticosteroids have shown acceptable outcomes. Systemic corticosteroids may provide temporary relief but have a high recurrence rate when used alone. In cases of necrosis, urgent debridement is required to prevent further complications.1,3

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A man in his 30s presented with a painful ulcer on the ventral aspect of the penile shaft that had appeared 3 months before. His medical history included recent unprotected sexual intercourse 2 months prior to consultation and recurrent self-healing ulcers on both the ventral and dorsal sides of the penis over the past 3 months. Physical examination disclosed discrete penile swelling with an indurated yellowish plaque diffusely involving the ventral surface. A well-circumscribed, round-shaped, 10 × 8-mm diameter, nonexudative ulcer on the more proximal area of the plaque was also noted (Figure 1A). In addition, 3 round-shaped scars, corresponding to previously resolved ulcerations, were observed on the penile dorsum. No regional lymphadenopathy or other mucocutaneous lesions were detected. Results of a complete standard laboratory workup was normal. Results of polymerase chain reaction for herpesvirus types 1 and 2,Treponema pallidum, andChlamydia, along with bacterial cultures of the ulcer, were all negative. Results of serology for syphilis, HIV, and hepatitis C and hepatitis B virus were also negative. A cutaneous biopsy obtained from the ulcer’s periphery was performed for histopathological examination and cultures (Figure 1B).
